name: Dennis Koshta
shortBio: I build LLM systems, AI tools, and interactive projects. I’m especially interested in AI safety and alignment.
aboutParagraphs: I tend to follow an interest by making something. Sometimes that means running an experiment to understand a model; sometimes it means making a game with strange geometry or a landscape you can compose music in. I like having something I can try, change, and learn from.

At UC Santa Cruz, I studied computer science and math, worked on classifying muscle signals with NeuroTechSC, and led a team building RL and LLM agents in the AIEA Lab. Since then, my engineering work has included retrieval systems, AI tools, and agent evaluation. I’m now at Bronco AI in San Francisco.

Led a four-person team working on reinforcement learning and LLM agents, including a Minecraft agent that could gather resources and craft items.
Co-founded an AI analytics platform and worked on product direction, full-stack development, and its private beta.

aboutSections.title: Why AI safety and alignment
paragraphs: The part of AI I keep coming back to is the gap between what we ask a system to do and what it actually learns to do. A model can pass a test without solving the problem we intended. An agent can report success when the work is incomplete. As these systems get more capable, understanding those gaps matters more.

That’s what motivates my experiments with training signals, automated checks, and model internals. I’m interested in useful ways to detect failures, improve oversight, and keep people in control. The questions are bigger than any one project here; the experiments are small ways to investigate specific parts of them.

aboutSections.title: How I approach projects
paragraphs: I like working across the whole project: the idea, the underlying system, and what it feels like to use. The creative projects give me room to explore that. Signal Garden connects music with an editable landscape; Impossible Rooms lets me play with spaces that couldn’t exist in a normal building.

I use Codex and Claude Code extensively to build and experiment. My part is choosing the direction, working through design decisions, testing the results, and deciding what needs another pass. Each project page explains the collaboration. For experiments, I also include what was measured, what didn’t work, and what the results can’t tell us.

aboutSections.title: Outside software
paragraphs: Math, biology, and physics—including quantum physics—are all subjects I enjoy learning about. Some of that curiosity finds its way into projects, like an orbital simulation or a procedural ecosystem, and some of it is just an interest in the subject itself.
Away from the computer, I’m into prog rock, cooking, and backpacking.
